candidates.attacker_control: Any request/DB/entity value interpolated with `${...}` (or an equivalent Content block) into an HTML attribute whose name starts with `on`, e.g. the documented `<span onclick="showName('${userName}')">`; the attacker supplies the value (e.g. `userName=');alert(1);//`).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified in source that (1) `on*` attributes do reach Escape.javaScriptAttribute via writeTagAttributeUserContent; (2) the code generator does call setContext with the attribute name for `on*` values (JavaCodeGenerator.java:316-324, KotlinCodeGenerator.java:346-354), so this is not a context-tracking gap; (3) no later escaping pass re-encodes the produced output (the escape writes directly to the underlying TemplateOutput); (4) `&` is escaped in htmlContent/htmlAttribute but deliberately absent for javaScriptAttribute, so the omission is specific, not a global convention; (5) docs explicitly present the onclick example as safely escaped, indicating the intended protection; (6) PreventInlineEventHandlers is opt-in only and not part of the default OwaspHtmlPolicy (OwaspHtmlPolicy.java:5-11). Browser character-reference decoding in attribute values and subsequent JS parsing is standard HTML behavior; it was not executed here.
candidates.impact: Cross-site scripting in the application origin when a victim triggers the element (e.g. click): session/token theft, actions as the victim, defacement. Requires a plausible but specific template pattern (inline event handler + user data inside a JS string), hence not a universal XSS in every jte app.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses ContentType.Html (default OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput) and renders user-controlled data inside an inline event handler attribute, with that data placed inside a JavaScript string literal (the exact usage documented in docs/html-rendering.md:99-106). A custom HtmlTemplateOutput that escapes `&`, or the optional PreventInlineEventHandlers policy / strict CSP without unsafe-inline, would mitigate.
candidates.root_cause: `gg.jte.html.escape.Escape.javaScriptAttribute` (jte-runtime/src/main/java/gg/jte/html/escape/Escape.java:66-86, switch at 73-82) escapes `'` (\x27), `"` (\x22), `\`, and control characters, but not `&`. It is selected for every attribute whose name starts with `on` (OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput.java:70-71). Because the emitted value is placed inside an HTML attribute in the response, the browser decodes character references in the attribute value before the event handler is compiled as JavaScript. An attacker value such as `');alert(1);//` therefore becomes a literal `'` in the DOM handler, terminating the template's JS string and injecting statements. In contrast, Escape.htmlAttribute (line 34) and Escape.htmlContent (line 15) do escape `&`; javaScriptBlock (script raw-text bodies) is not affected because character references are not decoded there, which shows the omission is specific to the attribute context.
candidates.title: JavaScript attribute escaping omits `&`, allowing HTML-entity decode to break out of JS string literals in `on*` attributes
candidates.trace: Template `<span onclick="showName('${userName}')">` -> TemplateParser recognizes the code part inside attribute `onclick` -> JavaCodeGenerator.onHtmlTagAttributeCodePart emits `jteOutput.setContext("span", "onclick"); jteOutput.writeUserContent(userName);` (JavaCodeGenerator.java:316-324) -> OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput.writeUserContent(String) (line 32) -> writeTagAttributeUserContent (line 65) -> attributeName.startsWith("on") -> Escape.javaScriptAttribute (line 71). With userName=`');alert(1);//` none of the escaped characters appear, so the raw entity is written; the response contains `onclick="showName('');alert(1);//')"`, the browser decodes the attribute to `showName('');alert(1);//')`, and the handler executes attacker script on the site origin.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no build, template render or browser was run (execution is out of scope). Exploitability depends on the app using ContentType.Html with an inline handler that embeds user data inside a JS string; no in-repo callers/tests confirm which templates downstream projects use. Test sources are absent from the snapshot, so no test asserts the intended escaping set.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS)

coverage_summary: Reviewed all modules present in the 230-file snapshot at the level of security-relevant flows: jte-runtime (TemplateEngine, TemplateLoader/RuntimeTemplateLoader, ClassInfo/Constants, StringUtils, escape package, html policies/support, output implementations, LocalizationSupport, BinaryContent, Template), jte (TemplateParser, TemplateCompiler, Java/Kotlin-independent code generators, JavaClassCompiler, Directory/ResourceCodeResolver, ContentProcessor/CodeBuilder, MigrateV1To2), jte-kotlin generator, jte-spring-boot-starter-2/3 (view resolvers, views, auto-configuration, properties), jte-models/native-resources/watcher, jte-maven-plugin and jte-gradle-plugin, jte-jsp-converter(-jakarta), jte-extension-api(-mocks), plus docs and poms. P1 index coverage: 227/230 files indexed, 167 Java files parsed with 1925 symbols/4002 call sites, no control-flow or data-flow analysis, semantic resolution not implemented and 2498 unresolved calls; index relations were used only for navigation and every cited edge was re-checked against source text. The snapshot contains no test sources (test/ modules and src/test are absent although pom.xml lists test modules), so expected escaping behavior could not be cross-checked against tests. No builds, tests, scanners or payloads were executed.
limitations: No runtime confirmation: browser HTML-entity decoding and JavaScript execution were reasoned from standard HTML behavior and source, not executed.

The candidate is condition-based: it requires an app template that puts user-controlled data inside a JS string literal in an inline `on*` handler; no downstream template files are present in the snapshot to confirm such usage.
Test sources are excluded from the snapshot, so the intended escaping character set and any regression tests could not be inspected.

The P1 index has no data-flow/control-flow and many unresolved calls; reachability from HTTP entry points is not established (jt e exposes render APIs; the Spring starters map view names to templates).
Build plugins, JSP converters and extension modules were reviewed for attacker-controlled input but not exhaustively line-by-line; they are build-time tools and no strong candidate was found there.
Because only one candidate may be submitted, the other XSS-adjacent leads listed in rejected_leads remain unconfirmed alternatives.

rejected_leads.lead: `a`/`href` javascript: mitigation is bypassable (OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput.java:66; StringUtils.startsWithIgnoringCaseAndWhitespaces in jte-runtime/src/main/java/gg/jte/runtime/StringUtils.java:8-25). The helper only skips leading whitespace, while browsers strip ASCII tab/LF/CR anywhere in a URL, so e.g. `java\tscript:alert(1)` renders and is executed on click; the check also only covers tag `a`/attribute `href` and misses other URL attributes.
rejected_leads.reason: Real incompleteness of a best-effort mitigation, but it is an undocumented filter over an app-supplied URL rather than the escaping contract; impact and prerequisites are comparable to but slightly more conditional than the selected candidate, so it was not chosen as the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Template calls inside HTML attribute values receive no context: TemplateParser allows `@template.x()` in Mode.Text inside an attribute (TemplateParser.java:315-321) while explicitly rejecting calls in script/style blocks (TemplateParser.java:246-249), and JavaCodeGenerator.onTemplateCall/KotlinCodeGenerator.onTemplateCall (JavaCodeGenerator.java:423-433, KotlinCodeGenerator.java:453-463) emit the call without `setContext`, so the callee's top-level user output is HTML-body escaped (quotes not escaped) while physically inside an attribute.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible attribute-context mismatch, but it needs an unusual template structure (template call inside an attribute value whose callee echoes user data at top level); not enough source evidence of real usage to select over the primary candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: DirectoryCodeResolver performs no name confinement: root.resolve(name) is used for read/exists/lastModified (jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/resolve/DirectoryCodeResolver.java:33-59), and ResourceCodeResolver concatenates the name into a resource path (ResourceCodeResolver.java:34-48); in on-demand mode a traversed file is compiled and rendered.
rejected_leads.reason: Path traversal/arbitrary-file-read only if an application passes attacker-controlled data as the template name; no in-repo caller or documented pattern does this, and ClassInfo name handling often fails such names, so evidence of attacker control is weaker.

rejected_leads.lead: `<style>` bodies use HTML-body escaping (OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput.java:57-63): `Escape.htmlContent` does not neutralize CSS metacharacters, so user data in a style block permits CSS injection (data exfiltration/UI manipulation).
rejected_leads.reason: Appears to be a documented-by-omission design limitation rather than incomplete implementation of a claimed protection; impact (CSS injection) is lower than script execution.

rejected_leads.lead: Spring Boot starter reactive auto-configurations can create an on-demand template engine (DirectoryCodeResolver + TemplateEngine.create, runtime compilation) when precompiled templates are not enabled, without the developmentMode guard present in starter-3's JteAutoConfiguration (ReactiveJteAutoConfiguration.java in starter-2 and starter-3).
rejected_leads.reason: Deployment/configuration weakness requiring an unusual production setup; not directly driven by attacker input and not a code-level injection flaw.

summary: Snapshot is casid/jte 3.1.16-SNAPSHOT (230 visible files; test sources are not included in the snapshot). I reviewed the runtime escaping/HTML output pipeline, TemplateEngine/TemplateLoader/CodeResolver path, template parser and Java/Kotlin code generators, Spring Boot starters, jte-models/native-resources/watcher, Maven/Gradle plugins and the JSP converters. The strongest source-supported issue is incomplete JavaScript-attribute escaping: `Escape.javaScriptAttribute` never neutralizes `&`, so an attacker-controlled value rendered into an `on*` HTML attribute (exactly the pattern demonstrated as safe in `docs/html-rendering.md`) can use an HTML character reference such as `'` to introduce a quote after the browser decodes the attribute value, breaking out of the JavaScript string literal and executing script (XSS). The P1 relation index confirms `OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput.writeTagAttributeUserContent` dispatches to this function and shows no other escaping layer for this path; because the index has no data/control-flow and tests were not in scope, this is a source-level lead, not runtime-confirmed.
